Algebraic loops

Source: vignettes/algebraic-loops.Rmd
algebraic-loops.Rmd
library(simcompR)

A feedback cycle made only of direct-feedthrough blocks defines a signal implicitly, y = f(y, u), at every instant. Such a cycle is an algebraic loop. A cycle that passes through an integrator, a delay or any other block without direct feedthrough is ordinary dynamic feedback and is not a loop.

Detection

Compilation builds the graph of direct-feedthrough dependencies and finds its strongly connected components. A component with more than one block, or a block wired to itself, is a loop. By default it is an error, with one cycle printed:

m <- sim_model("loop")
sim_add_block(m, "constant", "u", value = 1)
sim_add_block(m, "sum", "s", signs = "+-")
sim_add_block(m, "gain", "k", gain = 2)
sim_connect(m, "u", "s", input = 1)
sim_connect(m, "k", "s", input = 2)
sim_connect(m, "s", "k")
sim_compile(m)
#> Error:
#> ! Algebraic loop(s) detected: every block on the cycle has direct feedthrough, so the outputs depend on themselves at the same time.
#>   k -> s -> k
#> Break the loop with a stateful block (integrator, unit_delay, ...) or compile with algebraic_loops = "solve".

simcompR never breaks a loop by inserting a hidden delay: that would change the mathematics silently.

Solving loops

With algebraic_loops = "solve" each loop is solved at every evaluation. The unknowns are the outputs z of the blocks in the loop, and the residual is F(z) - z, where F evaluates the loop blocks once from the guessed outputs. Newton’s method with a finite-difference Jacobian and a backtracking line search drives the residual below loop_tol.

plan <- sim_compile(m, algebraic_loops = "solve")
plan
#> <sim_plan 'loop'> 3 block(s), 0 continuous state(s), 0 discrete state(s), 3 signal element(s)
#> Execution order: u > k > s
#> Algebraic loops (solved by Newton iteration):
#>   {k, s}
r <- sim_run(plan, c(0, 1), times = c(0, 1))
sim_signal(r, "s")   # s = 1 - 2 s, so 1/3
#> [1] 0.3333333 0.3333333
sim_diagnostics(r)$loop_residuals
#>      time     residual iterations
#> [1,]    0 5.551115e-17          2
#> [2,]    1 5.551115e-17          2

The residual and iteration count at every recorded time are part of the result diagnostics. A loop that does not converge is an error, never a silently inconsistent result.

A nonlinear loop

y = \cos(y) has the unique solution y \approx 0.739085:

nl <- sim_model("cos_loop")
sim_add_block(nl, "math", "c", fun = "cos")
sim_add_block(nl, "gain", "y", gain = 1)
sim_connect(nl, "c", "y")
sim_connect(nl, "y", "c")
r <- sim_run(sim_compile(nl, algebraic_loops = "solve"), c(0, 1), times = 1)
sim_signal(r, "y")
#>         y 
#> 0.7390851

Loops without a solution

y = y + 1 has no solution. The Jacobian of the residual is singular and the run fails with an explanation:

bad <- sim_model("inconsistent")
sim_add_block(bad, "constant", "one")
sim_add_block(bad, "sum", "s")
sim_connect(bad, "one", "s", input = 1)
sim_connect(bad, "s", "s", input = 2)
sim_run(sim_compile(bad, algebraic_loops = "solve"), c(0, 1))
#> Error:
#> ! Simulation failed at t = 0: Algebraic loop {s} at t = 0: singular Jacobian at the current iterate. The loop may have no unique solution, or the start is at a stationary point; give a starting value with sim_compile(loop_guess = ).

Several solutions and starting values

y = 4 / y has the solutions 2 and -2. Newton’s method started from zero cannot move (the residual is not even defined there), so the run fails and says how to fix it. A starting value given with loop_guess selects the solution:

two <- sim_model("two_roots")
sim_add_block(two, "constant", "four", value = 4)
sim_add_block(two, "divide", "y")
sim_connect(two, "four", "y", input = 1)
sim_connect(two, "y", "y", input = 2)
sim_run(sim_compile(two, algebraic_loops = "solve"), c(0, 1), times = 1)
#> Error:
#> ! Simulation failed at t = 0: Algebraic loop {y} at t = 0: the residual is not finite (NaN or infinite) at the starting point; give a starting value with sim_compile(loop_guess = ).
pos <- sim_compile(two, algebraic_loops = "solve", loop_guess = list(y = 1))
neg <- sim_compile(two, algebraic_loops = "solve", loop_guess = list(y = -1))
c(sim_signal(sim_run(pos, c(0, 1), times = 1), "y"),
  sim_signal(sim_run(neg, c(0, 1), times = 1), "y"))
#>  y  y 
#>  2 -2

Every solve starts from the same value, so results never depend on the history of the solver’s trial points.

Loops inside dynamics

Loops can sit inside a continuous model. Here \dot x = s with s = -x - s, so \dot x = -x/2:

dyn <- sim_model("dynamic_loop")
sim_add_block(dyn, "integrator", "x", initial = 1)
sim_add_block(dyn, "sum", "s", signs = "--")
sim_add_block(dyn, "gain", "k", gain = 1)
sim_connect(dyn, "x", "s", input = 1)
sim_connect(dyn, "k", "s", input = 2)
sim_connect(dyn, "s", "k")
sim_connect(dyn, "s", "x")
r <- sim_run(sim_compile(dyn, algebraic_loops = "solve"), c(0, 4),
             rtol = 1e-10, atol = 1e-12)
max(abs(sim_signal(r, "x") - exp(-sim_times(r) / 2)))
#> [1] 4.410894e-11

Every derivative evaluation solves the loop, which costs extra function evaluations. When possible, solve the loop by hand (here, replace the loop by a gain of 1/2) or break it with a physically meaningful state.

Feedthrough that depends on parameters

Whether a state-space block has direct feedthrough depends on its D matrix. A plan whose D changes from zero to nonzero through sim_set_params() is analyzed again, so a new loop is never missed. See vignette("compilation").

Limits

  • Loop solving uses a dense finite-difference Jacobian; it is meant for small loops.
  • Switching blocks inside a loop take their mode from the solved signals at every segment boundary (repeated until the modes settle) and keep it inside the segment, where their crossing functions locate changes.
  • Consistent initialization of differential-algebraic systems is not covered here; see the roadmap.
